chapter_theme: At the end of Vatsa kandam a ball-play contest is won by Mananigai after Dattai's side is beaten; the king marries her, Dattai's anger yields to worship, and he later marries Virisikai by sacrifice, ending as the husband of four chaste queens ruling in peace.

cast.role: Padumai's maid who opens the ball-play
a woman who strikes three thousand
Dattai, Vasavadatta, the king's first queen
Mananigai, daughter of the Kosala king, who wins the contest and becomes a queen
the ladies who ride to the wedding temple
the king of Vatsa (named by titles in these verses)

224.reading: A maid of Padumai takes up the ball with her bamboo-slim broad hand, strikes it fifteen hundred times with her ornaments ringing like a peacock dancing in the rain cloud, and steps back.
224.nuance: The maid's name is written across a word break in line 4; the verse opens a ball-play contest whose two sides are only implied.
224.event: Padumai's maid takes the ball, strikes it fifteen hundred times and then withdraws.

225.reading: Dattai's friend Visuvalekai comes forward and strikes the ball two thousand times with both hands, her ornaments and anklets sounding.
225.event: Visuvalekai, Dattai's friend, strikes the ball two thousand times with both hands.

226.reading: Another friend of Padumai, a woman of dark long hair and spear-like eyes, takes the ball and strikes it five hundred times along her forearm to the clash of her bangles.
226.event: A friend of Padumai strikes the ball five hundred times along her forearm.

227.reading: A woman named Ariyai takes the ball and strikes it three thousand times, and after that the company of Dattai no longer looks at the gathering with pleasure.
227.nuance: The verse does not say which side Ariyai plays for; the loss of heart in Dattai's company in the last line suggests she is of the other side.
227.event: Ariyai strikes the ball three thousand times, and Dattai's company loses heart.

228.reading: With no one left to answer the score, Dattai sits troubled and joyless; the verse then names a new woman, Mananigai, the daughter of the king of Kosala, of unspeakable chastity.
228.nuance: Mananigai is introduced as the daughter of the king of Kosala and praised for her chastity before she does anything, so the poem marks her virtue first and her skill second.
228.event: Dattai sits dejected, and Mananigai, the Kosala king's daughter, is introduced.

229.reading: The poet describes Mananigai limb by limb, from forehead like a young moon to waist, thighs and feet, with images of the bamboo, the parrot, the golden pot and the plantain.
229.nuance: Line 3 and 4 images are heavy with rare words and may be damaged; the order of the limbs is only partly clear.

230.reading: Mananigai, who has come to Dattai on some business, cannot bear to see her defeated, bows to her with respect and tells her the rules of ball-play of many kinds.
230.nuance: The verse says she came for another reason and does not name it; her instruction of Dattai, not her own play, answers the defeat.
230.event: Mananigai bows to the defeated Dattai and tells her the rules of ball-play.

231.reading: Taking a large ball, Mananigai strikes it with both hands in turn, sends it running, hides it in the garland, and plays it like a snake that has just given birth, bowing and rising as she plays.
231.nuance: Line 3 is hard: the gloss of the ball hidden in a garland and of the snake dance is mine; the numeral in line 1 reads as thirty-two.
231.event: Mananigai plays the ball with both hands, running it, hiding it in the garland and making it dance.

232.reading: Mananigai plays on, dancing the round and standing dances while the sweat on her brow is wiped on her silk and her slender waist bends.
232.event: Mananigai keeps up the dance-steps of ball-play, sweating and bending at the waist.

233.reading: All who watch are amazed, saying they have never seen the like, and ask whether she is a woman of the sky, a goddess of the lesser order, a woman of the nether world or a vidyadhara, and that there is none like her on earth.
233.nuance: Line 3 is damaged (தரிவுவிச்சை), and the classes named are read as a goddess of the vyantara order and a woman of the bhavana world.
233.event: The onlookers wonder at Mananigai and ask whether she is a divine woman.

234.reading: When she takes up the ball on her fingertips and strikes it, her bangles ring and the balls rise through sky and earth like whirlwinds.
234.nuance: Line 1 is corrupt (காந்தணன் ஒருமுன் கைக் கன்னியன்); only the ringing bangles and the whirlwind simile are clear.
234.event: Mananigai strikes the ball so that it rises through sky and earth to the sound of her bangles.

235.reading: As the woman strikes the ball ten times, her anklets and small bells ring, the pearl strands sway on her young breasts, and bees and honey-gatherers hum above her hair.
235.event: Mananigai strikes ten, her ornaments ringing and bees gathering about her hair.

236.reading: The sound of her anklets and bracelets is sweeter than any music or the songs of the gods, and wins the king's heart.
236.nuance: The last line is unclear (கூடகமனத்தினற்கு மரனினிய னாயினன்); I read only that the king is won and turns kind.
236.event: The sound of Mananigai's ornaments wins the king's heart.

237.reading: Saying that, rising and falling, there is none but she in all the world who plays so before ladies and a king, she strikes the ball eight thousand times with her forehead-hand.
237.nuance: The count is the highest of the contest and beats Ariyai's three thousand in verse 227 by a wide margin; line 2 on the king and women is not clear.
237.event: Mananigai strikes the ball eight thousand times, exceeding every earlier score.

238.reading: The women ride a she-elephant to the great wedding temple, where the king takes the dark-eyed Mananigai in joy, and Dattai hears of it and is seized with anger.
238.nuance: The verse turns the contest into a courtship: the king reaches Mananigai through the skill she showed. Dattai's anger is her first response to the second queen.
238.event: The party rides to the wedding temple, the king unites with Mananigai, and Dattai hears and grows angry.

239.reading: At dawn Dattai brings flowers and worships the king's feet while Mananigai stands joyless; the king speaks to her to comfort her, and then marries her with full rites.
239.nuance: The speech of consolation is only reported, and the verse does not say what the king told her. Dattai's worship follows her anger of verse 238 with no word on how it was resolved.
239.event: Dattai worships the king with flowers; he comforts Mananigai and marries her fully.

240.reading: With the three queens present the king marries Virisikai, like a bunch of flowers set among the garland, by a proper fire sacrifice.
240.nuance: The marriage is by vedic sacrifice (வேள்வி), as the verse names it; the work does not comment on that rite in a Jain epic.
240.event: The king marries Virisikai in the presence of his three queens, by sacrifice.

241.reading: The four chaste women keep a place in the king's heart and he enjoys them without lack, while firm kings come to pay tribute and bow at his feet, and the king rules all his friendly land.
241.nuance: The picture of an enjoying, tribute-taking king closes the chapter with no sign of the renunciation that the epic's own tradition would later expect.
241.event: The king lives happily with his four wives and rules while other kings bring tribute.

links.note: Verse 230 brings in Mananigai, named in verse 228, to meet Dattai's defeat.
links.teaches: The newcomer introduced by name and rank as a chaste princess in verse 228 first acts only in verse 230, when she steps in to answer the defeated Dattai.

links.note: Mananigai's eight thousand strikes answer the despondency of Dattai's party in 228.
links.teaches: The gloom with which Dattai sits defeated in 228 is not lifted by Dattai herself but by a stranger's play, which shows the poem making skill the cause of reversal.

links.note: Her eight thousand outdoes Ariyai's three thousand, the score that had silenced Dattai's side.
links.teaches: Ariyai's three thousand is shown as the peak only until Mananigai's count, so the contest's score is a ladder and each verse's number is meaningful only against the one before.

links.note: In 239 Dattai, angry in 238, comes with flowers to worship the king and the second marriage is completed.
links.teaches: Dattai's anger at the news is not allowed to stand; the next dawn shows her worshipping the king anyway, so the epic treats a first wife's resentment as a passing mood rather than a break.

links.note: The four chaste women of 241 are Dattai, Padumai, Mananigai and Virisikai; Virisikai's marriage in 240 completes the number.
links.teaches: The count of four in 241 only makes sense once 240 adds Virisikai to the three queens, so the closing contentment is the sum of the marriages.

links.note: Both verses list the tricks of ball play, hiding the ball in a garland and making it dance like a snake.
links.teaches: Two Jain epics share one catalogue of ball tricks, so the hidden-in-garland and snake-dance play is a conventional set of skills, not either poet's invention.

links.note: Both show a queen's resentment at a king's divided heart, but Dattai's anger ends in worship and the Pandya queen's sulk ends in the king's blindness.
links.teaches: The Silappathikaram makes a queen's sulk the opening that lets the goldsmith's lie in, while here the first queen's anger is quickly absorbed; the same domestic feeling has opposite consequences.

links.note: Both close on a king with tribute-paying kings around him, but Civakan turns away from it in dharma and Udayanan stays in it.
links.teaches: The same picture of a king whom others serve ends in renunciation in the Cintamani and in enjoyment here, so the minor epic's close is not the great epic's close.

links.note: The Kural's wife calls her husband a philanderer because all women feast on him with their eyes; Dattai's anger at his second marriage is the same grievance.
links.teaches: The epic shows what the Kural's grievance leads to when the husband is a king who really does take another wife, so the complaint is tested rather than only voiced.

gains.a: Dattai's anger is given a name and a ground that the verse itself leaves unspoken.
gains.b: The wife's complaint, which in the Kural stays a lovers' quarrel, is carried to a real second marriage and a quarrel that is settled by her bowing.

source_issues: Verse 224: the maid's name Ayirapathi is split across a word break.
Verse 229: lines 3 and 4 are heavily compounded and may be damaged.
Verse 231: the numeral in line 1 reads thirty-two.
